name: Earlobe reduction/repair

lead: Earlobe repair and reduction give neater, more even lobes. Repair mends lobes torn or split by heavy earrings, trauma or gauged piercings; reduction shrinks or repositions oversized or protruding lobes. The tidier lobe is visible once healed.
Published sources are mostly surgical technique papers and small case series. One paper on cosmetic repair notes that piercing-related complications are rising with the popularity of body piercing.

paras: Surgeons remove scar or excess tissue and close the lobe with designs such as Z-plasty, L-plasty, V-flap or double-flap, chosen to avoid notching of the lobe edge. It is a minor procedure done by a plastic surgeon or similar specialist.
Notching at the lobe rim is the outcome the techniques aim to avoid. One L-plasty series reported no complications, and larger controlled studies were not found.

angle.text: A minor procedure that mends torn or split earlobes from heavy earrings or gauges, or shrinks oversized lobes, leaving them neater and more even. The tidier lobe is visible once healed. The literature is mostly technique papers and small case series.

lead: Earlobe repair and reduction are surgical procedures that reshape or mend the earlobe. Repair addresses torn or split lobes, often from heavy earrings, trauma or gauged piercings, while reduction addresses oversized or protruding lobes.[1][2][3]

Published sources are mostly surgical technique papers describing Z-plasty, L-plasty, V-flap and double-flap closures intended to avoid notching of the lobe edge.[4][5][6][7][8] A paper on cosmetic repair notes that piercing-related complications are rising with the popularity of body piercing.[3]
infobox: Torn or cleft lobe, stretched piercing, protruding or large lobule

paras: Wikipedia notes that torn lobes may be sutured and cleft lobes usually need a tissue graft.[1] Published techniques include a half Z-plasty,[5] an L-plasty series of 9 cleft-earlobe patients in which one repair had slight notching,[6] a V-flap alternative to Z-plasty described in 1984,[7] a double-flap technique,[8] and L-specular and double-round plasty.[9] A guidewire punch technique has been described to remove unwanted epithelial tracts left by piercings.[10] One author outlines 11 surgical pearls and describes immediate repiercing.[3]

Wikipedia calls lobe repositioning the hardest part of otoplasty and describes the Gosain technique and other methods to pull a protruding lobe toward the head.[1] Grokipedia describes excising a wedge or a few millimeters of fat and skin for a protruding lobule.[2]

Studies are small retrospective series and technique reports. A retrospective study of 9 patients with 11 cleft earlobe repairs, mean follow-up 5.5 months, found moderate notching in both simple repairs and slight notching in 1 of 9 L-plasty repairs, with no complications.[6] Other publications describe half Z-plasty, V-flap, double-flap and specular techniques.[5][7][8][9] No randomized trials were found.
